speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If need be, I invite Members to seek clarifications following my response.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Leong Mun Wai asked about the lessons learnt and outcomes of the Gifted Education Programme, or GEP.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The GEP has generally delivered good student outcomes in the past 40 years, with many students being stretched intellectually and developing holistically.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: GEP alumni have made significant contributions in diverse fields such as public service, medicine, academia, arts, entrepreneurship and technology.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Many GEP alumni are also active leaders in the community and social sectors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, there were also some students who felt weighed down by the expectations to excel, or could not cope with the rigour of the programme and lost interest in learning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There were also students who were selected for the programme but decided not to join.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Over this time, the Ministry of Education (MOE) has gained useful lessons and experiences in developing higher-ability learners.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have observed that while some students showed high abilities in multiple areas, there are also some students who showed passion and strength in specific single areas, such as in English or Mathematics.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students may also present strengths and potential at different points in their educational journey, rather than at a single point in time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These observations are in line with international research.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Concurrently, over the years, our primary schools have expanded their capacity in nurturing high-ability learners.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, all primary schools have teachers trained to identify and develop high-ability learners in both cognitive and social-emotional domains.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Hence, it is timely to update our approach to develop higher-ability learners.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And instead of being selected at a single point, students can join these programmes at any time during their upper primary years.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want to work with parents to have the proper mindset to allow students to blossom at their own pace, rather than be hot-housed or rushed to be admitted at a particular entry point.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The new approach also gives students the option to exit the programme or modules at any time, if they find them unsuitable or wish to pursue other interests, without the stigma of having failed to meet the expectations after being labelled as gifted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Denise Phua, Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Mariam Jaafar asked about different aspects of our new approach.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students who can benefit from further stretch beyond school-based programmes can attend after-school modules at nearby schools.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These after-school modules will bring like-minded peers together to interact and inquire more deeply on selected topics.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will ensure a good geographical spread of schools offering these programmes, so that they are accessible to all eligible students regardless of where they study.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Together, these programmes will provide higher-ability learners a more customised suite of development opportunities according to their interests and strengths.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They aim to cultivate curiosity, creativity and a love for learning in students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They are not designed to help students perform better in mainstream examinations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Neither is the aim to introduce higher subject levels ahead of time, which would still be bounded by the core curriculum and examination requirements.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I wish to assure Mr Leong Mun Wai, Ms Mariam Jaafar, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Mohd Fahmi that MOE will support schools and teachers to deliver this new approach effectively and consistently.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: MOE will guide them in using multiple sources of information to identify higher-ability learners.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These holistic assessments will include the students’ academic abilities and social-emotional readiness for the programme.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: MOE will continue to support our primary schools by providing more curriculum resources and professional learning for teachers to support the cognitive and social-emotional development of our higher-ability learners.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, we will continue to train teachers to understand the cognitive and affective traits of higher-ability learners, establish a classroom climate that encourages exploration, creativity and personal reflection for these students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There will be platforms for schools to share best practices on how they design, implement and monitor their school-based programmes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Dr Wan Rizal asked about resource allocation and Mr Louis Chua asked about class sizes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: MOE will continue to resource schools according to the learning needs of their students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While the typical class size in primary schools can go up to 40, the pupil to teacher ratio of 15 is comparable to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, schools already have the flexibility to group students for learning based on their needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, Foundation-level classes are typically smaller, with between 10 and 20 students.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I want to thank the Minister for the courage to look into changing the GEP.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It has been a sacred cow for many years in our MOE system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is also aligned with the Minister's vision, which I fully support, of making education pathways to be more student-centric and to bring out the best in each student.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My question to the Minister is: why not go all the way out to let students pick the subjects in which they can have most passion and ability for, at the highest level that they can pursue and attain?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Why is there still a need for labelling a programme as for gifted or not gifted, especially if we have the concept that giftedness could be in academics, sports, arts, leadership and so forth?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Why not go all the way and scrap all these labels and let each perform to his or her best, and study to his or her best?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am just concerned that if we continue to now decentralise the GEP to every school for the top 10%, then, would it be possible that it would get back to the old situation where there is a so-called elite class, and families and students will chase that class, and there is this Express stream possibility and the rest?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My question to the Minister is: why not go all the way, according to his vision that many support?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, why do we not allow students to pick their subjects?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want to combine their areas of strength with their areas of interest, in order for them to be enrolled in certain classes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is to have our education system, where possible, tailored to the respective needs of our students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But, of course, it would not be possible for us to run some of these classes just on the basis of interest, without an assessment of the ability – which brings me to my second point.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For all of us familiar with teaching and teaching pedagogies, we know that it is actually very tough to teach to the average where you have a class of very diverse abilities, from very high-needs students to very high-ability students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This will also help to alleviate the workload of our teachers instead of having them to teach to the average across a class with very diverse abilities in a finite period of class time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having said that, we come to the third point – which is, we all know that when our children develop, it is not just about learning academically in one area or another area.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want to make sure that their social-emotional development commensurates with their academic development.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the same time, beyond those subjects and areas, there will always and there must always be opportunities for them to mix with students with diverse backgrounds, with different abilities so that as they grow up, they also learn to live and work with people with different abilities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the approach that we are adopting to make sure that on one hand, we want the benefits of focused teaching and learning; on the other hand, we want a diversity of backgrounds, of people so that our students can mix and grow up together.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will certainly take into consideration the students' interests and abilities in assigning them to the classes that will best bring out their potential.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In relation to the new higher-ability programme, can I check again with the Minister if there will be a change in the form class size for those who are in this programme and those who are not in this programme?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One of the learning points or points highlighted by many GEP students, past and present, and even parents, is that they shared that the smaller class size of the GEP is one of the key features.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I think many educators themselves have also expressed a desire for a smaller class size so that they would be able to, as the Minister said, develop each child to his or her highest potential holistically and I think having that smaller class size will enable them to better do so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, I think many of us talk about class size.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But actually, if we visit our schools, as I do regularly, you will find that in today's Singapore's education system, we have class sizes, from a few like five, all the way to 40.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It all depends on the needs of the students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For the higher-needs students on both ends of the spectrum, we will tend to have smaller class sizes in order to cater to their diverse needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, we have a range of class sizes, there is no one-size-fits-all class size because it all depends in the needs of the students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, for some of the very high-needs students, we have pull-out classes for one-to-one or one-to-two.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having said that, let me take a step back and explain how we manage this issue of class size with the finite resources that we have.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The main and most important determinant of the quality of our education outcome is the quality of our teachers and how we support them to enable them to use the most effective pedagogical tools for the different types of classes.
Assuming that this is the average class size that we have resources for the entire system, how do we resource it?
We cannot change the average very much because, in every society, there are only so many quality teachers that we can recruit.
For the higher-need students, we have smaller class sizes to cater to their needs.

But on the other hand, we must learn to leverage technologies to allow other class sizes that are not so high-needs, in order for the students to do learning on their own to complement what the teachers are teaching them.
So, today, actually, there is no such thing as an average class size in our school system.
But in reality, we have a range of class sizes, from the smaller class sizes to the bigger class sizes, according to the specific needs of our students.
And, of course, I would like to thank everyone for your support for MOE to have more resources to support our teachers.
But we are very cognisant that the quality of our education outcome is much more dependent on the quality of our teachers and the support that they get, rather than just a class size issue alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am very sensitive to the Minister's response that the class size alone is not a determinant and it is imperative that we also allow quality teachers to address our students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, as he acknowledged, it is, and I quote, "difficult to teach to the average".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While we have dedicated significant resources to both ends of the distribution, the lower-ability as well as the higher-ability end, effectively, what we are saying when we have a large class size is that we do not believe that there is enough diversity of ability within the middle of the distribution for us to actually need to have smaller class sizes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am wondering if the Minister would agree with me that, actually, if we have smaller class sizes, there can be greater tailoring also for the needs of the middle-ability students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We can all agree that the quality of our teachers is most important.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We can also all agree that there is a finite number of quality teachers within any system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: MOE will be very happy to be able to recruit many more quality teachers if we can do so and we will continue to do so and expand our recruitment, whether it is from the young graduates to the mid-career people, to expand our teaching pool.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But no matter how many teachers we have, it comes back to this concept – we are not applying all the teaching resources evenly to all classes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Which class requires what class size depends on the needs of the students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It does not matter whether it is one end of the spectrum or the other end of the spectrum or in the middle.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Then the question is: how do we break what I call the "trilemma" of any public education system: achieve quality at scale, achieve speed of innovation and achieve affordability?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because you can go through it in your mind, in most public education systems, you can, at most, get two out of three.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If you have quality and speed, chances are that it is not so affordable.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If you have quality and it is affordable, chances are that you cannot scale.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Adaptive training system will be the way that we can break the conventional trilemma, where we want to achieve quality, speed and affordability.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What is an example of an adaptive training system?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Young people play games up to the level that they are comfortable with and they can be repeatedly stretched until they reach the next level.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These same technologies are available today on the market where students with high abilities to high needs can all be taught at a level with the aid of the computer.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will give a simple example: English language learning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They need time, they need many more practices in order to get some basic fundamentals right.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the past, it was one teacher to one child in NorthLight School.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, the teacher can supplement his or her abilities with technology.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The child can repeat the same exercise multiple times without overly taxing the teacher, who has to focus on other students and, yet, at the same time, the child does not have to feel pressurised that he is impinging on the teacher's time nor the stigma that he is repeating the lessons.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That same technology can be used for the middle- or the high-end students, where people use the same technology to improve their language proficiency, according to the levels that they are at.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, for us, I think we need to transcend this debate about whether class size or not class size.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, in one of my speeches recently, which I have shared with the National Institute of Education (NIE), we give ourselves this challenge: if in medicine, in the future and now, we can produce a batch of one, that means medicine customised to the one person; in education, can we, one day, asymptotically, arrive at the holy grail, whereby our students can have the pedagogy of one?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, whether it is one end of the curve or the other end of the curve or somewhere in the middle, we will try our best to complement our best teaching resources with the best technology in order for us to mass customise accordingly to bring out the best in each of our students.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I would request for questions to be succinct and answers to be succinct as well.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Allow me to have a little bit of a preamble.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, try to keep it short in the interest of time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: An ideal education system is one that allows a child to learn over time at his own pace, based on his ability and interest.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: A high-ability child should be given more stimulation, while a slow-learning one should be given more time to develop.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I acknowledge that MOE has slowly moved towards that in recent years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But like what Member Ms Denise Phua had said just now, I think we can do more.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The problem with our current education approach is that it is still very much focused on sorting out the students and labelling them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That has a lot of implication on the subsequent academic advancement of the child.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As a result, parents play to the rules and pressure their kids, often at a very young age.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, my question to the Minister is: does the Ministry have plans to reduce the sorting and examination pressure currently experienced by our students?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our aim to allow different students to be in different groups of roughly the same ability is not to stigmatise them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is to enable them to be in a learning environment that best suits them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Every examination – and we have been repeating this – is not a competition to compete with other people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I said in my Adjournment Motion yesterday, we want our students to keep having the mental model to surpass themselves, rather than surpass other people in an exam.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To surpass themselves in life, rather than to surpass other people in an exam.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How we respond, as a society, will complement what MOE is teaching.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Whether a student feels stigmatised or not, we all each have a responsibility.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we do not change our mindset, if we label our students because of the classes that they go to, then we have failed our students and no amount of policy or structural change will help us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The reason why we have Full Subject-based Banding (FSBB) is because we have moved away from grouping students of average abilities together.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We do not look at people and say: you are gifted, means you are gifted in everything; you are average, means you are average in everything.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We know that different people have different strengths and this is the spirit behind FSBB.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the spirit behind what we do in the education system: allow every student to understand each and every of their strengths and weaknesses; know and have in them the mindset that, "while I may be strong in something, I need not be strong in everything and I must respect other people who are strong in other things that are different from me".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Together, with our diversity of strengths, we can build a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Apologies to Mr Liang, I will give it to Mr Darryl David.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Minister mentioned that the students who are going to be selected for the enhanced abilities stream, we should not see this enhanced abilities stream in a way as a kind of streaming that will allow them added advantage for their mainstream subjects.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, could the Minister share how MOE would design the curriculum of the programme, such that the students who are selected for this programme, that it will not be a programme that will allow them to have added advantage, say, in their English and Mathematics at the Primary School Leaving Examination, should they be selected for the English and Mathematics enhanced stream, or the enhanced programme for these two subjects?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They, on their own, would have done very well for their conventional exams.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our role is to provide them with more opportunities to stretch their abilities in different dimensions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If someone is selected for the English programme, that person may be highly, more able in languages and we would like to expose them to different genres of literature, expose them to different kinds of linguistic issues that might challenge them, might stretch their abilities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want everyone to understand that when you are chosen, you have certain abilities in certain areas.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But that does not mean that they have abilities in all areas.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, neither should the student feel, "I must excel in all areas just because I have been chosen".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have thought very hard and I have not come to an answer yet, because I think whenever we use the phrases "higher-ability programme", "gifted programme", there seems to be a suggestion that, somehow, if there is a high, there must be a low.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If you are gifted, there must be a non-gifted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Maybe we should just reframe our mind and say there are different types of abilities, different dimensions of abilities; not whether it is high, whether it is low, left, right, front, centre.
